strengths: Addresses a well-motivated limitation of prior theory-based RL (VGDL's restricted language and slow simulator-based planning) with a sensible architectural idea: separating a stable, general-purpose PDDL abstraction layer from a flexible, LLM-synthesized low-level Python transition model, combined via bilevel (Fast-Downward + BFS) planning.
Clear worked examples (Figs 2-5, 9) that concretely illustrate how exploratory subplans and abstraction-labeled replay buffers help the LLM localize and fix errors in the synthesized world model.

Demonstrates large gains in API-call efficiency and wall-clock planning time over an LLM-only planning baseline (GPT-o1) across four domains, and an ablation isolating the specific contribution of bilevel/hierarchical planning to runtime.

The zero-shot transfer of a world model learned in one version of Baba is You (KekeCompetition) to a visually distinct variant (Baba is AI) is an interesting and relatively convincing demonstration of the compositional reuse the framework is meant to enable.
The paper is generally clearly written, with a thorough related-work discussion that accurately situates the contribution among TBRL, bilevel planning, and LLM-for-planning literatures.
weaknesses: The PDDL abstractions (operators/predicates) are hand-designed per domain by the authors, and in some cases (e.g., Sokoban's push_to_hole with the boxes_stuck predicate) they appear to encode substantial task-specific solution structure rather than generic, human-like priors; this significantly undercuts the central claim that the system's sample efficiency stems primarily from learning a low-level model that 'grounds' pre-existing general abstractions, since much of the hard reasoning is arguably baked into the hand-crafted operators themselves.

Evaluation is based on very small numbers of levels/trials per domain (often n=1 run per level despite LLM sampling temperature 0.7), with no repeated trials, variance estimates, or statistical testing, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported API-call counts, success rates, or runtimes.

The main comparison pits TheoryCoder (using GPT-4o) against an LLM-only baseline using a different, more expensive reasoning model (GPT-o1); while the authors justify this choice, it confounds model capability with architectural differences and weakens the validity of the head-to-head comparison.

No quantitative experimental comparison to the most directly relevant recent baselines discussed in related work (e.g., WorldCoder, Dainese et al.'s Python world-model synthesis, or EMPA itself), despite EMPA being repeatedly referenced as the prior TBRL system whose weaknesses motivate this work; claims that TheoryCoder solves games 'EMPA struggled on' are not backed by a reproduced EMPA baseline or numbers in this paper.
The 'Progress (%)' metric in Fig. 11 is not clearly defined or justified methodologically (how partial progress is scored per domain), limiting interpretability of a headline result.

Reproducibility is hampered by an apparently incomplete/placeholder code repository link and by the reliance on closed, non-deterministic commercial LLM APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-o1) whose behavior may drift over time, which is not discussed as a limitation.

The framing invoking human cognitive plausibility (e.g., 'humans already possess the abstract operators') is asserted rather than empirically supported, and sits somewhat uneasily with the heavy reliance on hand-engineered, domain-specific PDDL files and on an LLM's general world knowledge, which is unlike a young learner encountering a novel game.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting extension of theory-based RL (TBRL) that combines hierarchical PDDL abstractions with LLM-synthesized Python world models, addressing two real limitations of prior TBRL work (restrictive VGDL theory language and slow planning).
The architecture and pipeline (Fig. 1-5) are clearly illustrated with concrete worked examples (e.g., the Baba is You 'form_rule' example), making the mechanism easy to follow.
The bilevel planning ablation (Table 3) convincingly shows that constraining low-level BFS search with PDDL sub-goals can yield large speedups (seconds vs. timeouts) on the specific tested levels.
The zero-shot transfer result from the KekeCompetition Baba is You variant to Baba is AI is a nice demonstration of the compositional/reusable nature of a code-based world model.
The writing and related work discussion (situating the work relative to TBRL, model-based RL, program synthesis, and LLM planning) is thorough and well organized.
weaknesses: Central claims of 'learning world models' are substantially undercut because the PDDL operators, predicates, preconditions/effects, and the checker functions that bridge abstract and low-level states are all hand-engineered per domain by the authors, not learned; the paper itself admits this in Section 3.3.1 and the limitations. Since these hand-crafted abstractions often already encode near-solution structure (e.g., 'push_to_hole' for Sokoban, 'move_between_bottleneck' segmenting Push Boulders 1 into rooms), much of the reported success and efficiency may be attributable to this injected domain knowledge rather than to the proposed learning/planning framework itself.

The comparison between TheoryCoder and the LLM-only baseline is confounded: TheoryCoder uses GPT-4o while the baseline uses GPT-o1, a stronger reasoning model. The paper frames TheoryCoder's use of a 'less powerful' LLM as a strength, but this makes the head-to-head comparison of architectures unfair and the reported efficiency/success gaps difficult to attribute cleanly to the proposed method.

The empirical evaluation is very small in scale: only 4-5 levels for Sokoban/Push Boulders 1, ~17 levels for BabyAI, and ~13 for KekeCompetition, with no multiple seeds/runs or variance reported for the main success/API-usage tables (only the runtime ablation is averaged over 5 runs). This makes it hard to assess the robustness and statistical reliability of the central comparisons.

No direct empirical comparison is provided against the most closely related program-synthesis world-model baselines discussed in the related work (e.g., WorldCoder/Tang et al. 2024, Dainese et al. 2024, AutumnSynth, Evans et al. 2021), nor against model-based deep RL methods (e.g., MuZero-style approaches) that were extensively motivated in the introduction and related work but never actually benchmarked.

The comparison to EMPA is only qualitative/anecdotal ('successfully applied to VGDL games EMPA struggled on') without any reproduced quantitative EMPA numbers in this paper, weakening the claim in Question 4 of the experiments section.
The 'Progress (%)' metric used in Figure 11 is not clearly defined (how partial progress is measured is not specified), making this headline result difficult to interpret or reproduce.
The code repository link in the paper is broken/incomplete ('https://github.com' with no further path), undermining reproducibility.

Given the heavy manual engineering per domain (operators, predicates, problem files, and natural-language domain descriptions provided to the LLM), the claimed generality and scalability of the approach is questionable, and the paper does not provide evidence that abstractions can be reused/learned across genuinely novel domains without human intervention, despite this being presented as a key motivation of the work.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated hierarchical extension of theory-based RL, combining hand-specified PDDL abstractions with LLM-synthesized Python low-level transition models and a bilevel (Fast Downward + BFS) planner; this addresses two concrete limitations of prior TBRL work (restrictive VGDL theory language and poor planning scalability).

The system is evaluated across a genuinely diverse set of domains (Baba is You/KekeCompetition, BabyAI, Sokoban, Push Boulders 1), including domains that are not expressible in VGDL and on which the prior TBRL system (EMPA) reportedly struggled, demonstrating broader applicability than earlier theory-induction agents.

Reported sample-efficiency (API call) and success-rate gains over a strong LLM-only planning baseline (GPT-o1, including a heavy-prompting variant) are large and consistent across all four tested domains, and the ablation of bilevel vs. flat planning shows dramatic runtime differences (in some cases orders of magnitude), supporting the core claim that hierarchical abstraction constrains and speeds low-level search.

The zero-shot transfer of a world model learned on KekeCompetition to the visually and syntactically different Baba is AI implementation is a compelling qualitative demonstration of the compositional, reusable nature of the synthesized Python theories.

The paper is clear about what is and is not learned (only the low-level transition function; PDDL operators/predicates are hard-coded), and the limitations section is honest about the reliance on hand-designed abstractions and the need for future work on learning abstractions and handling stochastic/continuous domains.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution ("agents that learn theories with high sample efficiency") is substantially undercut by the fact that PDDL predicates/operators are hand-engineered separately for every domain (Figs. 6b, 7b, 8b, 10b); the paper does not ablate how much of the reported gain over the LLM-only baseline comes from this injected domain-specific structure versus the Python world-model synthesis or the bilevel planning mechanism itself, making it hard to isolate the source of TheoryCoder's advantage.

Evaluation is small-scale and not statistically robust: most tables report single-run API-call counts and success/failure per level with no repeated trials, confidence intervals, or variance estimates (only the runtime ablation in Table 3 is averaged over 5 runs), which limits confidence that the observed differences are not due to noise in LLM sampling (temperature 0.7).

The comparison to EMPA is only qualitative ("successfully solved VGDL tasks where EMPA struggled") without a quantitative side-by-side table of success rates, sample efficiency, or wall-clock time on the same levels, weakening the claim relative to the stated goal (Question 4) of directly benchmarking against prior TBRL work.

The sole baseline is an LLM-only planner (GPT-o1); there is no comparison to other relevant neurosymbolic or program-synthesis world-model approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., WorldCoder, AutumnSynth, Dainese et al.), nor an ablation of TheoryCoder without any high-level PDDL structure (i.e., LLM-synthesized flat/low-level world model plus planner only), which would more cleanly isolate the value of the bilevel/hierarchical design versus simply having an explicit code-based world model.

The domains studied are small, deterministic grid worlds; the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this, but the significance of the contribution for the stated goal of matching human-like learning in more complex/stochastic/continuous settings remains speculative and untested.

Minor presentation issues: notation is introduced somewhat informally and inconsistently (e.g., D vs. R_p/R_a vs. D_p/D_a for replay buffers), and some claims (e.g., "stratified learning strategies" improving planning, or comparisons to human hierarchical planning) are asserted without direct empirical or human-behavioral data in this paper, despite the framework's strong claims of cognitive plausibility.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and important limitation of prior theory-based RL (TBRL) systems: restrictive theory languages (VGDL) and non-scalable planning. Combining PDDL-based abstract planning with LLM-synthesized Python transition models is a sensible and reasonably novel architectural contribution.

Experiments span a diverse set of domains (VGDL games Sokoban/Push Boulders 1, BabyAI/Minigrid, and the more complex Baba is You via KekeCompetition and Baba is AI), providing a broad testbed relative to much of the TBRL/program-synthesis literature.

Direct, apples-to-apples comparisons against a strong LLM-only baseline (GPT-o1), the original TBRL system (EMPA), and a related program-synthesis agent (WorldCoder) show consistent and often large improvements in sample efficiency (API calls), task success, and computational efficiency (bilevel vs. ablated planning time in Table 4).

The paper includes an honest failure-mode analysis (Section 4.7) showing cases where TheoryCoder's world model overgeneralizes (e.g., "goop is always dangerous") and cannot solve levels requiring the abstraction to be violated. This is a valuable, non-cherry-picked limitation discussion.
A control experiment addressing training data contamination (Section 4.8, custom game) strengthens confidence that gains are not simply due to memorized game logic in GPT-4o's training data.
Reasonably detailed algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) and example prompts in the appendix aid reproducibility of the core mechanism.
weaknesses: The high-level PDDL abstractions (operators/predicates) are hand-designed per domain by the authors, not learned or synthesized by the agent. Given the paper's own analysis (Section 4.4) shows these abstractions are often the single most important factor in both computational and sample efficiency, this substantially undercuts the central claim of a more general, scalable TBRL agent — most of the "theory" that matters is still hard-coded, with only the low-level grounding learned. This is acknowledged in the limitations but arguably deserves more prominent framing and quantitative disentanglement (e.g., how much success/efficiency comes from abstraction design vs. LLM-based low-level synthesis).

Many core results (Tables 1, 2, 5, 6, 8) appear to be single-run outcomes with no reported variance across seeds, despite the paper itself noting in Section 4.7 that TheoryCoder can get "stuck" and fail in some runs of the same environment. This creates tension with claims like 100% success rates in Table 3 and makes it hard to assess robustness/statistical reliability of the main comparisons.

The LLM-only baseline (GPT-o1) is capped at 5 retries/6 API calls per level, which may not reflect its full planning capability; additionally, the baseline is not given the same iterative code-based world-model mechanism, making the comparison illustrate LLM-only planning weaknesses more than isolate the specific contribution of bilevel/hierarchical structure per se (though the WorldCoder comparison partially addresses this by controlling for code-based world modeling).

No ablation isolating the effect of the abstraction-labeled replay buffer / hierarchical refinement versus a flat, non-hierarchical program-synthesis refinement loop on success rate and sample efficiency (only wall-clock planning time is ablated in Table 4); this leaves open how much of the sample-efficiency advantage (not just planning speed) is attributable to bilevel planning versus simply having good hand-crafted goals/exploration heuristics.

The comparison to EMPA (Table 3, Fig. 6) uses different learning/architecture assumptions (EMPA learns its theory from scratch within VGDL, whereas TheoryCoder's abstractions and language are far more expressive and partially hand-given), so the efficiency comparison, while suggestive, is not fully controlled.

The strong cognitive-science claim that the specific PDDL abstractions used are ones "humans playing them for the first time already possess" is asserted without human behavioral evidence in this paper, weakening the paper's framing as a model of human learning specifically (as opposed to purely an engineering system).

Presentation has minor issues: inconsistent/duplicate figure references (e.g., "Fig. 4" used for both a table and a PDDL figure), some typographical errors, and dense related-work sections that could be tightened to leave more room for deeper analysis of the main experiments.

strengths: The core architectural idea—combining hand-specified PDDL abstractions with LLM-synthesized low-level Python transition models in a bilevel (hierarchical) planner—is a sensible and interesting engineering combination that plausibly addresses two known bottlenecks in prior TBRL work (restrictive VGDL theory language and slow value-based planning).

The empirical comparisons are broad in scope, spanning VGDL games (Sokoban, Push Boulders 1), BabyAI/Minigrid, and Baba is You (KekeCompetition), and include comparisons against several relevant baselines (EMPA, GPT-o1 direct planning, WorldCoder).

The paper includes a thoughtful qualitative failure-mode analysis (Section 4.7) showing where the learned world model overgeneralizes (e.g., 'goop always causes death'), which is an honest and informative limitation discussion.
A dedicated experiment to rule out training-data contamination using a newly designed custom game is a good methodological practice that many similar LLM-agent papers omit.
The figures (2-5, 9-11) clearly illustrate the learning/refinement loop and make the mechanism of exploratory-plan-guided model revision easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution—that the agent 'learns' theories more flexibly than prior TBRL—is undercut by the fact that the PDDL operators, predicates, and the checker functions mapping abstract to low-level states are all hand-designed per domain (explicitly stated: 'the only remaining computational problem is planning' once abstractions are hard-coded). This means most of the structure that drives success is injected by the experimenter, not learned, which is a significant gap between the claimed contribution ('more powerful learning') and what is actually demonstrated.

Statistical rigor is weak: almost all headline results (API call tables, success-rate tables, learning-efficiency comparisons) appear to come from single runs per level with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds reported, despite LLM outputs being stochastic (temperature 0.7 is used). This makes it hard to assess whether the large reported gaps (e.g., 24.5× API reduction) are robust or cherry-picked/lucky runs.

The baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: TheoryCoder uses GPT-4o while the LLM-only baseline uses the more powerful GPT-o1, and the EMPA comparison numbers appear to be drawn from the original EMPA paper rather than re-run under matched conditions/metrics, raising reproducibility and fairness concerns.

The GPT-o1-only baseline is a fairly weak strawman for 'LLM-based planning': it is not given code-writing/tool-use ability, which is known to substantially help LLM agents at planning and spatial reasoning tasks; a fairer comparison would include an LLM agent with tool use or chain-of-thought code execution rather than only text-based direct action outputs.

The domains studied are all small, deterministic, fully observable 2D grid worlds; the claims about scalability and generality to 'large domains' and 'diverse and challenging games' are only weakly supported given the modest scale and lack of any stochastic, partially observable, or 3D setting (acknowledged in limitations but this substantially limits the significance of the contribution).

The mathematical formalism in Section 3.2/3.4 (Eqs. 1-4, classical planning preliminaries) adds little rigor or insight beyond restating the algorithm already described in prose and Algorithm 1, and reads as padding rather than substantive theoretical contribution.

Despite the paper's motivation being grounded in human cognitive theories of learning, no human behavioral data are collected in this work; all human-comparison claims rely on citing prior EMPA/Tsividis et al. results, which is a step removed from directly validating the cognitive plausibility claims made in the introduction.

The ablation of 'bilevel planning' is limited to computational runtime effects (Table 4) rather than an ablation isolating how much of the sample-efficiency advantage is attributable to the (hand-crafted) abstractions themselves versus the LLM's code-synthesis capability, leaving the key comparative claim (Question 3/4 framing) only partially addressed.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap in theory-based RL: VGDL's restricted theory language and EMPA's slow value-iteration planning. The proposed fix (Python-based low-level theories synthesized by an LLM, combined with hand-specified PDDL high-level abstractions and a bilevel BFS/Fast-Downward planner) is a sensible and reasonably novel architectural combination.

Evaluation spans a genuinely diverse set of domains (VGDL Sokoban/Push Boulders 1, BabyAI, KekeCompetition Baba is You, and a custom contamination-free game), and includes multiple relevant baselines/comparisons (LLM-only GPT-o1 with both minimal and 'heavy' prompting, EMPA, and WorldCoder), which strengthens the case that the approach generalizes beyond a single benchmark.

Ablations are informative and directly support the causal claims: removing bilevel abstractions substantially increases (or times out) planning time (Table 4), and abstractions are shown qualitatively to matter for both sample efficiency (Sokoban's boxes_stuck predicate) and for guiding LLM refinement toward the correct part of the code.

The paper is unusually candid about failure modes (Section 4.7): it shows concrete cases where the learned world model overgeneralizes (e.g., 'goop causes death') and fails on levels requiring the agent to violate previously learned rules, which is a valuable and honest limitations analysis rather than a superficial one.

The contamination check (Section 4.8) using a newly designed game not seen in GPT-4o's training data is a good methodological practice that pre-empts an obvious confound in LLM-based synthesis evaluations.
weaknesses: The PDDL operators, predicates, and the 'checker' functions bridging abstract and low-level states are all hand-designed per domain, not learned. This substantially narrows what the system actually 'learns' (only the low-level Python transition function) relative to the paper's framing of general-purpose, reusable abstractions, and the limitations section itself acknowledges this hand-engineering is 'tedious' and unresolved — yet the abstract/intro somewhat oversells the generality gained over VGDL-based theories.

Sample sizes per domain are very small (4–5 levels for the VGDL games, 13–17 for BabyAI/KekeCompetition), and most results (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8) report single-run outcomes with no variance/error bars, despite LLM sampling temperature of 0.7 introducing stochasticity; only the runtime comparison (Table 4) is averaged over multiple runs. This limits confidence in the magnitude of reported gains (e.g., '24.5× reduction in API usage').

The main baseline (GPT-o1, an LLM given text state and asked to output plans/actions directly) is a fairly weak point of comparison for the specific claim that explicit code-based world models help — it is not given comparable scaffolding (e.g., self-consistency, tree search, or explicit stepwise simulation), and the paper concedes GPT-o1 even underperforms with 'heavy' prompting that hands it the ground-truth transition model, suggesting the baseline's failures may reflect general LLM planning weaknesses rather than isolating the specific benefit of the proposed hierarchical world-model approach.

Different LLMs are used for TheoryCoder (GPT-4o) versus the baseline (GPT-o1), which confounds method with base-model capability; while the authors argue GPT-o1 is 'more powerful,' this choice makes it harder to cleanly attribute performance differences to the architectural contribution versus model differences.

Despite heavy motivation from human cognition and theory-based learning in the introduction and related work, no human behavioral data or comparison is presented in this paper (unlike EMPA, which was directly validated against human learning curves); the claim that PDDL abstractions used are 'analogous' to human intuitive abstractions is asserted rather than empirically supported.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on versioned, closed-source commercial APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-o1) whose behavior can drift or be deprecated over time, and the paper does not report code/data release plans, seeds, or full hyperparameter/prompt variability analysis beyond the example prompts in the appendix.

The technical novelty relative to closely related prior work (WorldCoder, Tang et al. 2024) is somewhat incremental — essentially adding a hand-specified PDDL abstraction layer on top of an LLM-synthesized Python world model — and the paper does not deeply analyze how sensitive results are to the quality/choice of these hand-crafted abstractions across domains beyond a few illustrative examples.
